content: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is a condition caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which progressively weakens the immune system. In advanced stages, individuals with AIDS are highly vulnerable to opportunistic infections and certain cancers. HIV is transmitted through bodily fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal fluids, pre-seminal fluids, and breast milk that contain the virus. As of 2018, approximately 37.9 million people globally were living with HIV, including 1.7 million children under the age of 15. That same year, 1.7 million new HIV infections were reported, and 770,000 people died from AIDS-related illnesses. Alarmingly, 8.1 million people living with HIV were unaware of their infection. Although antiretroviral therapy (ART) has significantly improved outcomes for people with HIV, there is no sterilizing cure due to the presence of latent viral reservoirs. ART can achieve a functional cure by suppressing the virus to undetectable levels in the blood, but it does not eradicate the virus entirely. Modern ART has dramatically reduced the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV/AIDS. Notably, there have been two documented cases of sterilizing cures following bone marrow transplants for cancer: the Berlin patient (Timothy Ray Brown) in 2008 and the London patient in 2019. HIV/AIDS classification systems, such as the Bangui definition and the 1994 Expanded WHO AIDS Case Definition, are used for epidemiological surveillance but are not always clinically precise. In resource-limited settings, the WHO staging system for HIV infection and disease, which incorporates clinical and laboratory data, is widely used. The CDC classification system, based on CD4 T-lymphocyte counts, is another primary method. Clinically, HIV-positive individuals may not have AIDS unless they meet specific criteria, such as a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of an AIDS-defining condition. HIV causes AIDS by depleting CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes, which are critical for immune function. The virus is acquired through sexual contact, exposure to contaminated blood, or mother-to-child transmission. After initial infection, HIV rapidly replicates and disseminates to lymphoid organs, leading to an acute phase characterized by high viral loads and a sharp decline in CD4 T-cell counts. Over time, the immune system deteriorates more gradually during the chronic phase of infection. HIV-induced CD4 T-cell death occurs through mechanisms such as cytopathic effects, syncytia formation, autoimmunity, and superantigen formation. HIV is a retrovirus belonging to the family Retroviridae and the genus Lentivirus, which are known for causing chronic and often fatal diseases with long incubation periods. There are two main subtypes: HIV-1 and HIV-2. HIV-1 consists of two single-stranded RNA copies enclosed in a conical capsid made of the viral protein p24. Its genome includes key genes such as gag, pol, env, tat, and nef, which encode structural and functional proteins. Critical enzymes for HIV replication include reverse transcriptase, which converts viral RNA into DNA, and integrase, which incorporates the viral DNA into the host genome. HIV is highly genetically diverse, with no two genomes being identical, even within the same individual, leading to its classification as a quasispecies. Acute HIV infection may be asymptomatic or present with a mononucleosis-like syndrome, including fever, fatigue, sore throat, myalgia, and lymphadenopathy. It must be differentiated from other conditions with similar presentations, such as acute toxoplasmosis, CMV/EBV infections, and viral hepatitis. AIDS should be considered in patients with symptoms of immunodeficiency or opportunistic infections and distinguished from other causes of immunosuppression, such as common variable immune deficiency (CVID), chemotherapy, steroid therapy, and severe malnutrition. HIV is a global pandemic, with the majority of AIDS-related deaths occurring in Sub-Saharan Africa. Despite advances in ART, access to treatment remains limited in many regions. In 2018, 23.5 million people were receiving ART worldwide. The primary mode of HIV transmission is unprotected sexual intercourse, but high-risk exposures include contaminated blood transfusions, needle sharing, childbirth, and receptive anal intercourse. Infectivity is closely linked to viral load and varies throughout the disease course. Early detection of HIV is critical for improving outcomes. In 2006, the CDC recommended routine HIV testing for all Americans aged 13–64 during healthcare visits, as well as prenatal HIV testing for all pregnant women. Rapid HIV antibody testing is advised for infants born to mothers with unknown HIV status, with immediate initiation of antiretroviral prophylaxis if the test is positive. Virologic assays are required to diagnose HIV in infants under 18 months, as maternal antibodies may interfere with antibody-based tests. HIV infection leads to a progressive decline in CD4+ T-cell counts, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections and malignancies. Without treatment, the median time from infection to AIDS development is 8–10 years. However, with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), morbidity and mortality have dramatically decreased. In areas with widespread access to HAART, life expectancy for newly diagnosed HIV patients approaches normal levels with full adherence to therapy. Opportunistic infections (OIs) are a hallmark of AIDS and include viral infections (e.g., CMV retinitis, mucosal HSV, varicella zoster), bacterial infections (e.g., tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex, syphilis), and fungal infections (e.g., cryptococcosis, mucocutaneous candidiasis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia). ART has significantly reduced OI-related mortality in countries where it is accessible. HIV co-infections, such as tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C, are common due to shared transmission routes. Screening for these infections is recommended in all HIV-positive patients. In pregnancy, mother-to-child transmission is the primary mode of pediatric HIV infection. ART during pregnancy, labor, and postpartum, combined with neonatal prophylaxis, reduces transmission rates from 25% to less than 2%. The treatment of HIV-infected children poses unique challenges, including adherence, drug resistance, and long-term complications. ART regimens aim to suppress viral replication, restore immune function, and improve quality of life. Major drug classes include NNRTIs, NRTIs, protease inhibitors, fusion inhibitors, CCR5 antagonists, and integrase inhibitors. Combination therapy with at least three agents is standard. HIV/AIDS has profound economic and societal impacts, particularly in heavily affected regions. The epidemic has left many orphans cared for by elderly relatives, and the lack of access to healthcare and ART exacerbates the burden. Research continues to focus on improving treatments, reducing side effects, and developing a vaccine.
